For each of 1,000 simulations, we sampled group-level parameters from the posterior to generate synthetic patient and control datasets (N = 1,000 per group). A logistic regression classifier was trained on one simulated dataset and evaluated on an independent test dataset, with the parameters of the two datasets drawn from non-overlapping halves of the posterior draws and participant ages resampled from the observed sample. We compared a model based on PHS threshold alone with a model combining threshold, response time, and confidence ratings, with interactions between each parameter and age included in both models. Because the simulated datasets are generated from the fitted model, this analysis quantifies how well the estimated group differences separate patients from controls.

Additionally, to examine whether PHS is associated with thermal sensitivity 21 and spatial integration processes related to spatial summation and lateral inhibition, 22 we tested a further two pre-registered regression models. PHS threshold and slope were each regressed on cold and warm detection thresholds and psychometric slopes, as well as measures of spatial summation (i.e., the difference in perceived intensity between stimuli of different spatial extents) and lateral inhibition (i.e., the difference in perceived intensity between stimuli with identical overall area but different spatial separation). All predictors interacted with the group status (patients vs. controls) to test whether these relationships differed between groups.

Results

Thermal stimulation

Individually-calibrated peak temperatures, minimum temperatures reached during the cooling phase, as well as thermal contrast values showed no credible differences between groups in any of the four conditions. Bayesian t-tests provided inconclusive to moderate evidence for equivalence (peak temperature: BF01 = 2.81-3.98; minimum temperature: BF01 = 2.01-3.43; thermal contrast: BF01 = 1.52-3.75). Per-condition and per-group values are presented in Table 1 and Figure S1. By design, I-1 corresponded to each participant's warm detection threshold and N-1 to their heat pain threshold.

PHS prevalence

PHS prevalence, defined as reporting at least one PHS response across all trials, was observed in 38 out of 42 (90.5%) healthy controls and 29 out of 32 (90.6%) patients (Figure 2A), with moderate evidence for no group difference (BF01 = 5.84). At the stricter criteria (at least 5 to 30 PHS trials), evidence ranged from inconclusive to moderate (BF01 = 0.64-3.73). The mean number of PHS trials per participant was 15.3 (SD = 10.8) for healthy controls and 13.1 (SD = 9.9) for patients, and the mean per-participant percentage of PHS trials was 28.6% (SD = 20.4) for healthy controls and 24.1% (SD = 18.3) for patients. PHS rates were slightly higher on trials with a 1.5 s plateau (healthy controls: 29.2% vs 27.2%; patients with DPN: 25.9% vs 22.0%).

To examine whether PHS varied as a function of peak temperature condition, we fitted a Bayesian mixed-effects logistic regression.

PHS occurred more frequently during the noxious conditions (N-1 and N-2) than the innocuous conditions (I-1 and I-2). Bayesian model comparison provided strong evidence against a condition × group interaction (BF01 = 11.77) and against any group effect on PHS rates overall (BF01 = 12.48), indicating that PHS prevalence and its modulation by peak temperature condition were comparable between patients and healthy controls (Figure 2B).

Thermal contrast, PHS, and perceptual uncertainty

To visualise how thermal contrast relates to PHS and to behavioural markers of perceptual uncertainty across groups, we divided thermal contrast into 10 equally spaced bins. For each participant we plotted the proportion of PHS trials per bin (Figure 2C), together with response times and confidence ratings across the same bins, separately for PHS and cold trials (Figure 2D). The computational model formalises these relationships as a psychometric function linking thermal contrast to the probability of PHS, with group-level parameters for threshold, slope, lapse and guess rates, and by linking response time The warm phase (red) ramps temperature above the 32 °C baseline and returns, followed by a cooling phase (blue) that decreases temperature below baseline. The thermal contrast (TC) is defined as the normalised difference between peak and minimum temperatures. (B) Trial timeline. Each trial began with a fixation cross during which the thermal stimulus was delivered (red border), followed by a detection phase in which participants pressed a button upon perceiving a change in sensation (blue border). Participants then reported the perceived temperature (cold or warm) and rated their confidence on a visual analogue scale (VAS) anchored from "Guess" to "Certain". Arrows indicate the corresponding variables: peak temperature, minimum temperature, choice response time (RT), and confidence rating. (C) Schematic psychometric curve relating thermal contrast to the probability of reporting a paradoxical heat sensation (PHS). The curve is parameterised by threshold (α), slope (β, grey curves vary β only), guess rate (γ, lower asymptote), and lapse rate (λ, 1 -upper asymptote). (D) Predicted profiles for two hypothetical perceiver types. An unsure perceiver shows monotonically increasing choice RT and decreasing confidence with increasing P(PHS), reflecting growing uncertainty. A true perceiver shows non-monotonic patterns driven by decision entropy: both choice RT and confidence peak/dip near the psychometric threshold, where stimulus ambiguity is maximal. and confidence to that probability estimate.

The unsure perceiver model characterises PHS perception

We evaluated four models that specified different combinations of perceptual profiles across groups: unsure perceiver profiles in both patients with DPN and healthy controls, true perceiver profiles in both groups, and models in which the two groups differed in their assigned profile (unsure perceiver in patients and true perceiver in controls, or true perceiver in patients and unsure perceiver in controls). Only the model assuming an unsure perceiver profile in both groups met the pre-specified convergence criteria. The remaining models did not meet the pre-specified convergence criteria despite additional attempts to improve model estimation (see Supplementary Materials). Because only one model could be reliably estimated, the pre-registered model comparison could not be performed. Nevertheless, the descriptive response patterns were consistent with the unsure perceiver profile. Together, these findings indicate that the unsure perceiver model provided the most plausible account of PHS responses in the present sample, although this could not be formally confirmed through model comparison. All subsequent analyses were conducted using the unsure perceiver model for both groups.

PHS threshold is increased in patients with DPN

The relationship between thermal contrast and PHS probability was characterised by four participantspecific parameters: threshold (the thermal contrast corresponding to the inflection point of the psychometric function), slope (governing the rate of increase in PHS probability with increasing thermal contrast), guess rate (the lower asymptote of the function, i.e. the probability of reporting PHS as thermal contrast approaches its lower limit), and lapse rate (one minus the upper asymptote, i.e. the probability of not reporting PHS as thermal contrast approaches its upper limit). The group-level effect (patients with DPN vs. healthy controls) on the PHS threshold was credibly positive (log-scale estimate = 0.33, 95% HDI [0.12, 0.57], P(θ > 0) = .998; Figure 3A), corresponding to approximately 39% higher thresholds in patients at the average age and indicating that they required greater thermal contrast to reach the midpoint of the psychometric function. Averaged across participants, posterior mean thresholds were .51 (SD = .20) in healthy controls and .80 (SD = .29) in patients with DPN, corresponding to an approximately 30 percentage-point rightward shift. Observed thermal contrast ranged from .03 to .99 in healthy controls and from .04 to .98 in patients, so the estimated midpoints of both groups fell within the tested range.

Posterior predictive checks showed that the model reproduced the observed relationship between thermal contrast and PHS in both groups, at the group level and for individual participants (Figures S2-S5).

The psychometric slope (per unit thermal contrast on the 0-1 scale; HC: 148 ± 116; DPN: 176 ± 181), guess rate (HC: .09 ± .12; DPN: .15 ± .16), and lapse rate (HC: .27 ± .07; DPN: .28 ± .06; i.e. PHS probability reached a maximum of approximately .73 at the highest thermal contrasts) were numerically similar between groups, although these parameters were not formally compared. Patients with DPN therefore required greater thermal contrast to elicit PHS, with no indication of a change in the shape of the psychometric function.

Higher PHS probability is associated with slower responses and lower confidence in both groups PHS probability was positively associated with response time (mean = 0.93, 95% HDI [0.45, 1.40], P(θ > 0) > .999; Figure 3B), indicating slower responses when the estimated probability of PHS was higher. Conversely, PHS probability was negatively associated with confidence (mean = -1.41, 95% HDI [-2.02, -0.74], P(θ > 0) < .001; Figure 3C), indicating lower confidence when PHS probability was higher.

We found no credible evidence of a difference between patients with DPN and healthy controls in response time (mean = 0.02, 95% HDI [-0.22, 0.25], P(θ > 0) = .56) or confidence (mean = 0.02, 95% HDI [-0.33, 0.36], P(θ > 0) = .56), after accounting for thermal contrast and PHS probability. Thus, group differences in PHS were not accompanied by detectable differences in response time or confidence once PHS probability was taken into account.

Classification of patients and controls using PHS parameters

PHS threshold discriminated patients from controls with modest accuracy (median AUC = .68, 95% CI [.55, .80], P(AUC ≤ .5) < .01). Adding response time and confidence ratings resulted in numerically similar classification performance (median AUC = .67, 95% CI [.53, .80], P(AUC ≤ .5) < .01). These findings indicate that the group difference is primarily reflected in the psychophysical threshold. Response time and confidence therefore provided limited additional information for diagnostic classification beyond the threshold estimate.

PHS, thermal sensitivity and spatial integration processes

Of the 74 participants, 63 (36 healthy controls, 27 patients) had complete data across the three tasks of the overall study (i.e., thresholds, PHS; spatial integration); one healthy control lacked valid thermal thresholds, and ten participants (five controls, five patients) lacked spatial integration data. The regression model predicting PHS threshold from group, thermal detection thresholds and slopes, spatial integration measures, and their interactions with group explained a significant proportion of variance relative to an intercept-only model (F(13, 49) = 3.37, p = .001, R² = .47, adjusted R² = .33), indicating that the combined set of thermal detection thresholds and measures related to spatial integration explained substantial variance in PHS threshold. However, no individual predictor or group interaction reached statistical significance, suggesting that this explained variance was not attributable to a specific sensory measure or differential relationship between patients and controls. Variance inflation factors in a main-effects model were low (all ≤ 1.6). In contrast, the model predicting PHS slope did not explain significant variance relative to an intercept-only model (F(13, 49) = 0.99, p = .47, adjusted R² ≈ 0), indicating that thermal sensitivity measures and spatial integration metrics did not predict how strongly PHS probability changed with increasing thermal contrast.

Discussion

The present study shows that patients with diabetic polyneuropathy (DPN) require greater thermal contrast to elicit paradoxical heat sensation (PHS), without changing how PHS is experienced. Using a preregistered Bayesian modelling approach, we identified three main findings. First, the unsure perceiver model was the only one of the four pre-registered models that converged, providing a plausible account of PHS in both patients and controls. This suggests that, for most participants, PHS is experienced as an uncertain and unusual sensory event rather than as a clear sensation of warmth. Second, patients with DPN required substantially greater contrast to experience PHS: the midpoint of the psychometric function was reached at approximately 51% thermal contrast in healthy controls and 80% in patients, reflecting a shift of the function. Third, response time and confidence showed similar patterns in both groups, suggesting that DPN affects the sensory signals giving rise to PHS rather than the uncertainty that accompanies it.

These findings extend those of Ehmsen et al., who used the same paradigm and computational framework across the healthy adult lifespan and found that the unsure perceiver model characterised PHS in younger and older adults. 6 The present study shows that this perceptual profile generalises to individuals with DPN. PHS was also common in both groups, with approximately 90% of participants reporting it on at least one trial and moderate evidence for no group difference. PHS is therefore not specific to neuropathy but reflects a general feature of thermosensory perception when warm and cold inputs are presented in close succession, accompanied by perceptual uncertainty whether or not the thermosensory system is affected by peripheral nerve pathology.

Despite this shared profile, the PHS threshold shifted in opposite directions in healthy ageing and in patients with DPN. Older adults required less contrast to experience PHS, reflected in a leftward shift of the psychometric function, 6 whereas patients with DPN required more, reflected in a rightward shift. In both cases the shape of the function was preserved, suggesting that ageing and DPN change the sensitivity of the thermosensory system while preserving its capacity to encode graded changes in contrast.

Ageing may lower the PHS threshold through a mild, predominantly cold-related decline in thermosensory function 21 or through changes in central processing, such as reduced cortical inhibition 33 or shifts in excitation-inhibition balance. 34 However, cold detection thresholds were not associated with PHS thresholds in our sample, and the present data cannot distinguish between existing accounts of PHS, such as disinhibition of warm-signalling pathways 9 or misattribution of degraded cold input to the warm channel. 6 In contrast, DPN may raise the threshold by weakening peripheral thermal signals. In the same participants, detection thresholds were elevated in patients with DPN, for warm (BF10 = 3.75) and, less conclusively, cold stimuli (BF10 = 1.76), whereas pain thresholds did not differ (BF10 ≤ 0.34) (data from Courtin et al., 21 reanalysed for the present sample). Damage to small-fibre pathways attenuates thermal input, 35 so that greater contrast is required to generate equivalent sensory evidence at central processing stages. Together, these opposite shifts suggest that susceptibility to PHS may vary non-monotonically with thermosensory loss: partial decline, as in healthy ageing, may facilitate PHS, whereas more advanced loss of afferents, as in DPN, may weaken the signals from which PHS arises. This interpretation is consistent with clinical studies linking PHS to thermal hypoesthesia 13 and showing that it can precede measurable thermal sensory loss. 14 The comparable PHS prevalence between groups differs from clinical studies reporting higher PHS rates in individuals with neuropathy than in healthy controls 14 or DFNS reference values. 10;13 This discrepancy may reflect methodological differences. In the thermal sensory limen (TSL) procedure used in quantitative sensory testing, the thermal contrast experienced by participants is not experimentally controlled but emerges from individual detection thresholds. 10;36 Patients with impaired detection therefore experience larger temperature changes during testing and, because PHS probability increases with contrast, 6;7 are more likely to report PHS. In contrast, the present paradigm introduced systematic variability in contrast within each participant by combining four individually calibrated peak temperatures with a subsequent cooling phase, so that the relationship between contrast and PHS could be characterised across a range rather than at a single threshold-dependent value. Under these conditions, prevalence was comparable between groups, although patients required greater contrast to experience PHS, suggesting that neuropathy alters sensitivity to contrast rather than overall susceptibility to PHS. Differences in the number of trials between paradigms may also contribute to variation in reported PHS prevalence across studies.

The absence of group differences in response time and confidence suggests that DPN acts primarily on the sensory input underlying PHS rather than on its perceptual interpretation: peripheral nerve damage can change the relationship between stimulus and sensation without changing how uncertainty is experienced once a perceptual judgement is made.

Most previous research on DPN has focused on the structural and physiological consequences of smallfibre damage, including reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density (e.g., 37;38 ), impaired peripheral nerve function (e.g., 25;26;39 ) and altered thermal thresholds (e.g., 11 ). Less is known about how peripheral nerve pathology shapes perceptual experience. Perception requires the nervous system to infer the most likely sensory state from incomplete and variable information, 40;41 and degraded peripheral input reduces the reliability of this evidence. Our findings extend this framework to thermosensation, showing that DPN alters the relationship between thermal contrast and PHS, consistent with less reliable sensory evidence.

Several limitations should be considered. First, the patient sample size was modest (N = 32), which may have limited sensitivity to detect small group differences in psychophysical parameters, response time and confidence. Second, only the unsure perceiver model met the pre-specified convergence criteria, so alternative models could not be formally compared using leave-one-out cross-validation; future work using larger samples and alternative model formulations may further characterise the mechanisms underlying PHS. Third, thermal stimulation was applied at a single site on the volar forearm, whereas DPN can affect body regions heterogeneously and typically affects the feet most severely. In addition, patients' individual sensory profiles, such as the presence of neuropathic pain or predominantly cold or warm sensory loss, may have influenced sensitivity to thermal contrast; larger samples are needed to test whether PHS differs between sensory phenotypes. Finally, the cross-sectional design and the absence of stratification by neuropathy severity mean that the proposed nonmonotonic relationship between thermosensory loss and PHS susceptibility could not be tested directly; longitudinal studies following individuals from incipient to established loss are needed.

Conclusion

This study provides the first quantitative characterisation of the psychometric relationship between thermal contrast and PHS in individuals with DPN.

Although overall PHS prevalence was comparable between patients with DPN and healthy controls, the thermal contrast required to elicit PHS was substantially higher in patients with DPN, who required greater thermal contrast to reach the midpoint of their psychometric function. This difference reflected a shift in threshold without a change in the shape of the psychometric function, suggesting that DPN reduces the strength of peripheral thermal signals while preserving the relationship between thermal contrast and PHS probability. Across both groups, the unsure perceiver model accounted for the key behavioural features associated with PHS perception, including slower responses and reduced confidence during PHS trials, supporting the characterisation of PHS as an inherently uncertain perceptual experience. These findings demonstrate the importance of distinguishing between PHS prevalence and sensitivity to thermal contrast and suggest that elevated PHS rates reported in neuropathy using standard clinical protocols may partly reflect the coupling between impaired thermal detection and PHS measurement. Modelling the stimulus-response relationship underlying PHS may therefore provide a complementary approach for characterising altered thermosensory processing in clinical populations.

Figure 1.

Figure 1. Task overview and theoretical framework. (A) Stimulation protocol for a single trial.The warm phase (red) ramps temperature above the 32 °C baseline and returns, followed by a cooling phase (blue) that decreases temperature below baseline. The thermal contrast (TC) is defined as the normalised difference between peak and minimum temperatures. (B) Trial timeline. Each trial began with a fixation cross during which the thermal stimulus was delivered (red border), followed by a detection phase in which participants pressed a button upon perceiving a change in sensation (blue border). Participants then reported the perceived temperature (cold or warm) and rated their confidence on a visual analogue scale (VAS) anchored from "Guess" to "Certain". Arrows indicate the corresponding variables: peak temperature, minimum temperature, choice response time (RT), and confidence rating. (C) Schematic psychometric curve relating thermal contrast to the probability of reporting a paradoxical heat sensation (PHS). The curve is parameterised by threshold (α), slope (β, grey curves vary β only), guess rate (γ, lower asymptote), and lapse rate (λ, 1 -upper asymptote). (D) Predicted profiles for two hypothetical perceiver types. An unsure perceiver shows monotonically increasing choice RT and decreasing confidence with increasing P(PHS), reflecting growing uncertainty. A true perceiver shows non-monotonic patterns driven by decision entropy: both choice RT and confidence peak/dip near the psychometric threshold, where stimulus ambiguity is maximal.

Figure 2.

Figure 2. PHS prevalence, distribution, and raw decision variables. (A) Prevalence of paradoxical heat sensation (PHS) as a function of the minimum number of PHS trials per participant, shown separately for healthy controls (HC; blue) and patients with diabetic polyneuropathy (DPN; red). Shaded areas represent bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals (CIs). (B) Distribution of participants reporting PHS across peak temperature conditions (I-1 and I-2: innocuous; N-1 and N-2: noxious), stratified by group. Stacked bars indicate the number of PHS trials per participant (1-3, 4-6, 7-9, and ≥10). (C) Mean proportion of PHS trials per participant as a function of binned thermal contrast (0-1), shown separately for HC (blue) and patients with DPN (red). Individual dots represent participant-level means per bin; error bars indicate 95% CI. (D) Mean response time (RT; seconds; top) and confidence ratings (visual analogue scale [VAS]; bottom) as a function of binned thermal contrast, shown separately for PHS (dark) and non-PHS/cold trials (light) within each group (HC: blue shades, left; patients with DPN: red shades, right). Error bars indicate 95% CI.

Figure 3.

Figure 3. Computational modelling reveals increased PHS thresholds but preserved perceptual uncertainty in patients with DPN. Each row shows results for a different model parameter: (A) PHS probability, (B) log response time, and (C) confidence. Within each row, the left panel shows group-average model predictions as a function of thermal contrast for healthy controls (HC; blue) and patients with diabetic polyneuropathy (DPN; red), with shaded ribbons representing the 60%, 80%, and 90% posterior prediction intervals. The middle panel shows subject-level posterior mean parameter estimates by group (±68% credible intervals) with lighter colours, as well as group-level mean parameter estimates (±95% credible intervals) with darker colours: PHS threshold (A), log response time intercept (B), and confidence intercept (C). The PHS threshold represents the thermal contrast at the midpoint of each participant's psychometric function (i.e., halfway between its floor and ceiling probability). The right panel shows the posterior distribution of the group effect (patients with DPN vs. healthy controls) on each parameter; dashed vertical lines indicate zero (no group difference). The threshold posterior (A) is credibly positive (95% HDI excludes zero), indicating a rightward shift of the psychometric function in patients with DPN. The response time (B) and confidence (C) posteriors overlap zero, indicating no credible group differences in these parameters.
